structure.rationale: The requester's 22-chapter syllabus is kept intact and in order: Part I frames the problem (files vs tables, platform history, what Iceberg is and is not); Part II builds the core model (three layers, snapshots, schema, partitioning, row-level change); Part III covers architecture and design principles (catalog, storage, openness, reliability, governance); Part IV applies them to use cases; Part V turns them into decisions. Each chapter follows the requester's shape: problem scene, concept, how it works (visual), design principle, use case, decision guidance.
structure.audience: Data engineers, analytics engineers, architects, technical leaders, and product managers who need to reason about lakehouse architecture, not run Iceberg commands.
structure.voice: thing-explainer: common words, one scene per chapter, technical terms introduced once in quotes.

claims.text: In the Hive table model that preceded Iceberg, a 'table' is a directory convention: a metastore tracks partitions, but the files inside each partition are discovered by listing storage at read time, so the table's contents are whatever files happen to be in those directories at that moment.

Splitting table state between a metastore (partition list) and the file system (file list) makes atomic changes across partitions impossible; a job rewriting several partitions can be observed half-applied by concurrent readers, and a failed job can leave half-written files that readers then count as data.

The pain is worst on object stores: Netflix, storing data on S3 rather than HDFS, found directory listings slow and (at the time) eventually consistent, renames non-atomic, and planning cost growing with the number of partitions and files — the direct motivation for designing Iceberg.

What users implicitly expect from a 'table' is what SQL databases have long provided: a defined schema that can evolve safely, consistent reads, atomic writes, row-level updates and deletes, queryable history, fast planning, and a named unit that access control and governance can attach to — none of which a bare folder of Parquet files provides.

The CIDR 2021 lakehouse paper identifies the consequences at industry scale: file-based data lakes created reliability, staleness and data-quality problems, which enterprises papered over with two-tier architectures that continually ETL lake data into a proprietary warehouse.

Iceberg's central move is to define the table as an explicit, versioned list of files recorded in its own metadata rather than as directory contents: a snapshot is the complete set of data files making up the table at a point in time, tracked through a manifest list and manifest files.

A change commits by writing a new metadata file and atomically swapping the table's current-metadata pointer in a catalog; writers use optimistic concurrency (retry on a stale base when rules allow) and readers keep using the snapshot they loaded, so reads are serializable-isolated and never see partial writes.

Because metadata carries the file list plus per-file partition values and column statistics, scan planning needs a fixed number of remote calls instead of O(partitions) directory listings, and files can be pruned without opening them.

Scene seed (grounded): two pipelines write to the same Parquet folder; one job dies mid-write, leaving a few part-files behind, and every dashboard that lists the folder now silently double-counts — in Iceberg the same crash leaves only unreferenced files, because data files are written in place and join the table only through an explicit atomic commit.

snippets.code:
# What storage sees              # What the table knows
s3://lake/sales/dt=2026-10-13/   metadata/v412.metadata.json  <- current pointer
  part-0001.parquet  (job A)       snapshot 9812: [files...]
  part-0002.parquet  (job A)       snapshot 9813: [files...]
  part-0003.parquet  (crashed B!)  # part-0003 never committed -> invisible to readers
snippets.note: Contrast between directory-as-table (crashed writer's file is 'in' the table) and Iceberg's metadata-defined snapshot; structure verified against the Iceberg spec's metadata/snapshot/manifest model.

pitfalls: Parquet is a file format, not a table format: it defines how bytes inside one file are laid out, and says nothing about which files together constitute the table.
Object stores are not file systems: renames are copies, listings are paginated API calls billed per request, and no multi-file operation is atomic — intuitions from HDFS or a laptop do not transfer.
Adding a Hive metastore does not fix consistency, because it tracks partitions, not files; any change within a partition is still invisible to the transaction model.
Even with Iceberg, files on storage are not automatically 'in the table' — tools that scan the bucket directly will see uncommitted and orphaned files that no snapshot references.

claims.text: Data warehouses deliver schema-on-write governance, ACID transactions and strong BI performance, but historically at the cost of proprietary internal formats, coupled storage and compute, high cost, data lock-in, and poor support for machine-learning and unstructured workloads.

Data lakes (HDFS in the 2010s, then cloud object stores) inverted the trade: cheap elastic storage of open files (Parquet, ORC) readable by any engine, but with no transactions, weak consistency, and chronic data-quality and reliability problems.

Most enterprises ended up with a two-tier architecture — land everything in the lake, then ETL curated subsets into a warehouse — which duplicates data, adds pipeline failure modes, makes dashboards stale relative to the lake, and doubles the security and governance surface.

The lakehouse, as defined in the CIDR 2021 paper (Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin, Zaharia), is data management on low-cost, directly accessible open storage that adds warehouse capabilities — transactions, governance, indexing-like performance — via a transactional metadata layer over open file formats; the paper reports Parquet-based lakehouses competitive with cloud warehouses on TPC-DS.

An 'open table format' is precisely that metadata layer as a published specification: a vendor-neutral contract for how data files plus metadata represent a transactional table, so any compliant engine can read and write it; Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi all emerged around 2017–2018 to fill this role.

Iceberg was created at Netflix by Ryan Blue and Dan Weeks to replace Hive tables on S3, whose split metadata model could not guarantee correctness or atomicity at Netflix's scale; it was presented publicly at Strata in 2018, open-sourced and donated to the Apache Software Foundation in November 2018, and graduated to a top-level Apache project in May 2020.

2024 marked industry convergence on Iceberg as the neutral standard: Databricks (creator of rival Delta Lake) acquired Tabular, the company founded by Iceberg's creators, in June 2024 (reported near $1B); Snowflake announced the open-source Polaris catalog for Iceberg the same week; and AWS launched S3 Tables with built-in managed Iceberg support in December 2024.

Convergence continued at the format level: Iceberg format version 3 — adding binary deletion vectors, row lineage, and a variant type — was approved by the Apache Iceberg community in 2025, with Databricks explicitly framing v3 as unification of Delta and Iceberg capabilities.

Scene seed (grounded): the nightly copy commute — data lands in the lake, an ETL job trucks a subset into the warehouse overnight, and when that job breaks Monday's revenue dashboard quietly shows Friday's numbers; the lakehouse removes the truck by making the lake itself the transactional system of record.

pitfalls: 'Lakehouse' names an architecture pattern, not a product — vendors apply the label to very different systems, so evaluate the properties (open format, transactions, multi-engine access), not the word.
An open table format does not by itself make your platform open: if the catalog, governance, or maintenance tooling is proprietary, the lock-in just moves up a layer.
The warehouse did not die — the shift is that storage and format opened up; most 'lakehouse' query engines are warehouse engines that learned to read external open tables.
Lake economics are not automatically cheaper: object-store request charges, metadata growth, compaction compute and duplicated copies during migration all cost real money.

claims.text: The project's own definition: 'Iceberg is a high-performance format for huge analytic tables' that 'brings the reliability and simplicity of SQL tables to big data' while 'making it possible for engines like Spark, Trino, Flink, Presto, Hive and Impala to safely work with the same tables, at the same time.'

Iceberg is a specification plus client libraries, not a running service: there is no Iceberg server process; a table is data files and metadata files in storage plus a current-metadata pointer held by a catalog, and libraries (reference Java implementation, plus Python, Rust, Go, C++) implement the spec inside whatever engine is reading or writing.

What it provides: table semantics (a schema with stable field IDs, partitioning as table configuration rather than directory layout), atomic commits with serializable snapshot isolation, versioned snapshots enabling time travel and rollback, safe schema and partition evolution, and column statistics for query planning.

What it does not provide: query execution or any compute, the storage itself, ingestion or ETL orchestration, BI dashboards, or scheduling — it sits between an object store below and query engines above, with a catalog holding the pointer that makes commits atomic.

The working mental model is four cooperating parts: data files (Parquet, ORC or Avro) that hold rows; metadata files (snapshots, manifest lists, manifests) that record exactly which files constitute each table version; a catalog that maps table names to the current metadata file; and any number of engines that read and write through that metadata.

'Iceberg replaces Spark' is a category error: Spark executes queries and Iceberg defines what the table is; they are complements, and Spark remains one of the main engines that reads and writes Iceberg tables.

'Iceberg is a database' is wrong in a precise way: it has no compute, sessions, or query optimizer of its own; it is closer to a database's storage/table layer unbundled from the engine and shared, so that many engines can treat the same files as one consistent table.

Iceberg targets large analytic tables with commit-granularity changes, not OLTP: the spec's goals are serializable isolation, planning speed, and scale for analytic scans, and row-level change support (delete files in v2, deletion vectors and row lineage in v3) exists to serve CDC, corrections and compliance deletes — not high-frequency single-row transactions.

Its performance story is about planning, not scanning: metadata lets a client plan a scan in a fixed number of remote calls and prune files via partition values and min/max statistics, but the engine still reads the surviving Parquet files — Iceberg makes engines waste less work rather than doing the work itself.

Scene seed (grounded): the shipping-container standard — Iceberg is the container spec, not the ship or the crane: Parquet files are the goods, manifests are literal cargo manifests saying what is aboard, the catalog is the port registry pointing to the current manifest, and Spark, Trino or Flink are interchangeable cranes; standardizing the container is what let every port and vessel interoperate.

snippets.code:
ENGINES   Spark | Trino | Flink | DuckDB | Snowflake   (compute: not Iceberg)
             |
CATALOG   db.sales -> s3://lake/sales/metadata/v412.metadata.json  (atomic pointer)
             |
METADATA  metadata.json -> manifest list (per snapshot) -> manifests (file stats)
             |
DATA      s3://lake/sales/data/*.parquet                (storage: not Iceberg)
snippets.note: The catalog -> metadata -> data resolution chain every read follows; layer structure and pointer-swap commit verified against the Iceberg table spec.

pitfalls: You cannot 'install Iceberg' as a standalone system — adopting it means choosing a catalog, at least one engine, and an owner for maintenance; the format is the contract between those pieces, not a product.
Iceberg does not maintain itself: compaction, snapshot expiration and orphan-file cleanup are jobs some engine must run, or tables degrade in cost and speed.

Reading the Parquet files directly and bypassing the metadata gives wrong answers — deleted rows reappear and uncommitted or orphaned files get included, because only snapshots define table membership.
A table is only as atomic as its catalog: the commit is the catalog's pointer swap, so a weak or bypassed catalog (e.g., path-only tables on S3) forfeits the concurrency guarantees.

claims.text: An Iceberg table is organized in three layers: a catalog (which maps a table name to the location of its current metadata file), a metadata layer (metadata.json files, manifest lists, and manifest files), and a data layer (immutable data files, typically Parquet, plus delete files), all but the catalog living as plain files in object storage.
The catalog's pointer to the current metadata.json is the single source of truth for a table's current state; whatever that pointer names is, by definition, the table.

The table metadata file (metadata.json) holds the table's schemas (with history), partition specs, sort orders, table properties, the current snapshot ID, and a log of snapshots; each snapshot in it points to exactly one manifest list file.

A manifest list is one Avro file per snapshot; each entry names a manifest file and carries summary metadata such as partition value ranges, so a planner can skip entire manifests whose contents cannot match the query filter.

A manifest is an immutable Avro file listing data files (or delete files), recording for each file its location, format, partition value tuple, record count, and column-level statistics (value bounds, null counts); engines use these to skip individual files without opening them.

The read path traverses the tree top-down: resolve the table in the catalog, read the current metadata.json, select a snapshot (current, or an older one for time travel), open its manifest list, prune manifests, open surviving manifests, prune files, then read only the surviving data files — pruning happens in two stages before any data is touched.

The write path is bottom-up: a writer first writes new data files, then new manifests, a new manifest list, and a new metadata.json, and finally commits by asking the catalog to atomically swap the table's pointer to the new metadata file; nothing is visible to readers until the swap succeeds, and existing files are never modified.

Commits use optimistic concurrency: the pointer swap is a compare-and-swap conditional on the metadata the writer started from still being current; a losing writer re-reads the new state, re-validates for conflicts, rewrites only metadata, and retries — no locks are held while data is written.

Because all coordination reduces to one atomic pointer swap in the catalog, many independent engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, etc.) can read and write the same table safely without talking to each other.

Scene seed: the metadata tree works like a publisher's chain from front desk to page — the catalog is the registry naming the current edition, metadata.json is that edition's table of contents, manifest lists are its chapter lists, manifests are per-chapter page indexes with summaries, and data files are the pages; a reader never wanders the stacks, which is why Iceberg planning never lists object-store directories and scales with metadata size, not file count.

snippets.note: Iceberg exposes its metadata tree as queryable metadata tables; verified against the Spark Queries docs (Inspecting tables section).

pitfalls: Equating the table with its storage directory: the directory can contain files from old snapshots, failed writes, or orphaned jobs — only the metadata tree defines which files are part of the table.

Deleting or moving files directly in object storage corrupts the table, because metadata still references them; all file removal must go through table operations (expire snapshots, remove orphan files).
Treating the catalog as a minor configuration detail: atomic commits depend on the catalog's compare-and-swap, so without a catalog there is no transactional table.
Forgetting that every commit writes a new metadata.json and manifests: very frequent tiny commits bloat the metadata layer and snapshot history unless maintenance runs.

claims.text: A snapshot is the complete state of a table at a point in time: the full set of data and delete files that make up the table as of one commit, reachable through that snapshot's manifest list.

Every change — append, overwrite, row-level delete, even compaction — produces a new snapshot and a new metadata file; nothing is edited in place, and the table keeps an ordered snapshot log of its history.
Consecutive snapshots share unchanged manifests and data files, so a new snapshot costs only the metadata for what changed, not a copy of the table.

Readers get snapshot isolation: a query plans against the snapshot that is current when it starts and keeps seeing exactly that state even if other writers commit mid-query; writers never block readers and readers never block writers.

Time travel queries select an older snapshot by ID (VERSION AS OF <snapshot-id>) or by time (TIMESTAMP AS OF <ts>, which resolves via the snapshot log to the snapshot that was current at that moment).

Rollback after a bad pipeline run is a metadata-only operation: procedures like rollback_to_snapshot and rollback_to_timestamp move the table's current pointer back to an earlier snapshot instantly, without touching data files.

Retention is explicit: expire_snapshots removes snapshots older than a threshold (default: older than 5 days, retaining at least the last 1) and physically deletes only files uniquely owned by expired snapshots, never files a surviving snapshot still references.
Each snapshot records a summary of its operation (append, overwrite, delete, replace) and counts such as files and records added or removed, so table history doubles as an audit trail.
Snapshots can carry named references — tags (fixed labels for audit points) and branches (independent lines of commits, used for write-audit-publish) — each with its own retention policy.

Scene seed: a snapshot is like a Git commit, and the parallel is structural, not loose — both are immutable pointers to a complete state that share unchanged content with their ancestors, both support tags, branches, and resetting a pointer to undo, and in both the 'current version' is just whichever commit the reference points at.

snippets.note: Snapshot-pinned reads by time or snapshot ID; verified against the Spark Queries docs and Tabular's cheat sheet (Trino uses FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF).
rollback_to_snapshot is metadata-only; expire_snapshots defaults: older_than = 5 days ago, retain_last = 1. Verified against the Spark Procedures docs.

pitfalls: Snapshots are not backups: they live in the same storage as the data, and once expire_snapshots runs (or someone deletes files underneath the table) that history is gone — disaster recovery still needs separate replication.
Never expiring snapshots means every rewritten or deleted file is kept forever, so storage and metadata grow without bound; retention must be an operated policy, not a default.

Timestamp-based time travel resolves to whatever snapshot was current at that wall-clock time, which is not guaranteed to be the snapshot a particular job actually read — pin snapshot IDs for reproducibility.
Rollback moves the current pointer but does not delete the bad snapshots; they remain reachable (and readable) until expired, and new commits after a rollback start a diverging history.

claims.text: Iceberg supports full in-place schema evolution: add, drop, rename, and reorder columns (including nested struct fields), and widen types (int to long, float to double, increased decimal precision).
Schema changes are metadata-only: each change writes a new schema version (with a schema ID) into table metadata, and no data files are rewritten — historical files are read through the new schema.
The mechanism is field IDs: every column, down to nested fields, is assigned a unique numeric ID when created, and readers resolve columns in data files by ID rather than by name or position.

The official docs state the guarantees as independence from side effects: an added column never reads an existing column's values, dropping a column does not change the values of other columns, renaming keeps values bound to the column, and a re-added column with a previously used name gets a fresh ID so old data cannot resurface under it.

Name- or position-based resolution — the Hive-era approach — is what makes evolution unsafe elsewhere: a rename becomes an implicit drop-plus-add, and dropping then re-adding a column can silently surface the old column's data; Iceberg's IDs exist specifically to close this class of bugs.

The logical schema and physical file layout are decoupled: old files simply lack new columns (read back as null, or as a declared default value in format v3), and dropped columns' bytes remain inside old files until those files happen to be rewritten.
Format v3 adds default column values, so a newly added column can present a backfilled value for all pre-existing rows without rewriting a single file.

Because schema versions are committed and logged like data changes, the schema behaves as a governed, versioned contract: every historical snapshot knows which schema it was written under, and schema history is auditable and time-travelable.

Scene seed: field IDs work like employee badge numbers in an HR system — people change names, titles, and desks (rename, retype, reorder) but payroll always keys on the badge number, and a new hire never inherits a departed employee's badge, so records can never be silently attributed to the wrong person.

snippets.note: The four everyday evolutions, all metadata-only; syntax verified against the Iceberg Spark DDL docs (ADD/RENAME/ALTER/DROP COLUMN).

pitfalls: A rename is physically safe but operationally loud: every downstream query, dashboard, and pipeline that referenced the old name breaks and must be updated — the table format protects data, not SQL.

Dropping a column neither reclaims storage nor scrubs values: the bytes stay in existing files (and in old snapshots) until files are rewritten and history expired — a compliance concern if the column held sensitive data.
Type changes only widen; narrowing (long to int, double to float) is not supported, so choosing overly narrow types early forces awkward workarounds later.

Reading the Parquet files directly with a non-Iceberg reader bypasses ID-based resolution entirely — such readers see old column names and dropped columns, which surprises teams that mix raw-file access with table access.

claims.text: Partitioning groups rows into files by shared partition values so that queries filtering on those values can skip everything else; at large scale it is the single biggest lever for how much data a query must touch.

In Hive-style partitioning, partitions are physical directories keyed by explicit columns: users must maintain an extra derived column (e.g. an event_date string computed from event_time), writers must compute its values correctly, and queries must filter on that partition column by name or they silently scan everything.

The official docs name the consequences: Hive cannot translate filters automatically, users who do not understand the physical layout get needlessly slow queries, incorrectly written partition values silently produce wrong results, and queries become coupled to the partition scheme so it cannot change without breaking them.

Iceberg's hidden partitioning declares partitioning as transforms over real columns (e.g. day(event_time)); Iceberg computes and stores the partition value for each file in metadata, and neither producers nor consumers ever see or manage a derived partition column.

The spec defines the transform vocabulary: identity, year/month/day/hour on timestamps and dates, bucket(N, col) (hash into N buckets, for high-cardinality keys), and truncate(W, col) (prefix/width truncation).

Queries filter on the source column (WHERE event_time >= ...) and pruning happens automatically, because Iceberg knows the transform relationship and converts predicates on the column into predicates on partition values.
Writers hand Iceberg raw column values and the library applies the transform at write time, eliminating the class of bugs where the producer's idea of the partition value disagrees with the table's.

Partition evolution is a metadata-only change: altering the partition spec creates a new spec with a new spec ID, new files are written under the new spec, old files keep their original layout, and the planner plans each file against the spec it was written with — no rewrite, no downtime, no broken queries.
Partitions are metadata, not directories: partition values live in manifests, so file paths are irrelevant to correctness and a table can mix several layouts across its history.

Scene seed: Hive partitioning is a mailroom that makes every sender hand-write the routing code on the envelope and every carrier memorize the shelf plan; hidden partitioning is the post office deriving routing from the address itself — senders write only the address (the raw timestamp), sorting is the system's job, and the mailroom can reorganize its shelves (partition evolution) without re-mailing old letters.

snippets.code:
CREATE TABLE prod.db.events (
  id bigint, event_time timestamp, device string)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_time), bucket(16, id));
snippets.note: Declaring transforms at create time; days()/bucket() syntax verified against the Iceberg Spark DDL docs (PARTITIONED BY with transforms).
ADD/DROP PARTITION FIELD change the spec for future writes only; verified against the Spark DDL docs and the evolution docs.

pitfalls: Carrying Hive habits into Iceberg — adding a string event_date column just to partition by it — reintroduces exactly the duplicated-column and wrong-value bugs hidden partitioning exists to remove.
Over-partitioning (identity on a high-cardinality column, or too-fine time granularity) explodes the number of tiny files and manifest entries, hurting both write and planning performance.
Partition evolution does not rewrite history: files written under the old spec keep the old layout, so queries spanning the change prune old data less effectively until it is optionally rewritten.

Wrapping the partition source column in an expression the engine cannot map to the transform (e.g. filtering on date_format(event_time, ...) instead of event_time itself) can defeat pruning — filter on the raw column.

claims.text: Analytical tables cannot stay append-only in practice: privacy deletions (GDPR/CCPA), corrections of bad source data, slowly changing dimensions, and CDC replication of operational databases all require row-level change; pre-Iceberg data lakes handled these by rewriting whole partitions.
Iceberg format v2 introduced row-level DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE as atomic snapshot commits, with two physical strategies: copy-on-write (COW) and merge-on-read (MOR).

Copy-on-write rewrites every data file that contains at least one affected row: reads stay simple and fast because files are always clean, but changing one row in a gigabyte file means rewriting the gigabyte — write cost scales with files touched, not rows changed.

Merge-on-read leaves data files alone and writes small delete files recording which rows no longer count; writes are cheap and fast, but every subsequent read must merge deletes with data, and read overhead grows with the number of uncompacted delete files.

Format v2 has two delete-file flavors: position deletes name exact rows (file path plus row offset — precise for readers but the writer must first locate the rows), while equality deletes record column values to delete (no read-before-write, favored by streaming CDC writers, but the most expensive for readers, which must compare values on every scan).

Format v3 replaces v2 position delete files with deletion vectors — one compact bitmap per data file, stored in Puffin files — cutting merge-on-read's read amplification; engines using equality deletes for streaming ingest typically convert them to vectors during maintenance.

As of late 2026, v3 is production reality, not a proposal: Apache Iceberg 1.10.0 (2025) brought v3 features to general availability, 1.11.0 (May 2026) is current, major platforms (AWS, Snowflake, Google) support v3 tables, v3 readers can read v2 tables, and the v2-to-v3 upgrade is one-way.

The strategy is configurable per operation via table properties (write.delete.mode, write.update.mode, write.merge.mode, each copy-on-write by default), so one table can, for example, use MOR for streaming deletes and COW for batch merges.

Compaction is MOR's other half: regularly rewriting data files with their deletes applied pays down the read debt, and the workload rule follows — COW for read-heavy tables with infrequent batch changes, MOR plus scheduled compaction for frequent or streaming changes.

Scene seed: copy-on-write is reprinting a book page whenever an error is found, so every future reader gets clean pages; merge-on-read is shipping the original book with an errata slip the reader must cross-check, and compaction is the next printing that folds the errata in — the same correction, paid for at press time or at reading time.

MERGE INTO prod.db.customers t
USING staged_changes s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
snippets.note: The canonical row-level upsert (CDC apply / SCD maintenance) as one atomic commit; MERGE INTO syntax verified against the Iceberg Spark writes documentation.
Per-operation strategy choice on one table; property names and copy-on-write defaults verified against the Iceberg configuration docs.

pitfalls: A DELETE statement does not erase bytes: the rows remain readable in older snapshots via time travel, and under MOR they remain inside current data files masked by delete files — compliance-grade erasure is a pipeline (delete, compact, expire snapshots, remove orphan files), not a statement.

Equality delete files can themselves contain the sensitive values they were written to remove (if the match key is, say, an email address), and column min/max bounds in manifests can also retain values.
Merge-on-read without scheduled compaction degrades silently: each uncompacted delete file adds read-time work until query latency collapses.

Choosing a strategy by fashion rather than workload — MOR 'because streaming is modern' on a read-heavy reporting table, or COW on a high-churn CDC feed — pays the wrong cost on every operation; measure read/write ratios first.

claims.text: An Iceberg catalog maps table names (namespace.table) to the location of each table's current metadata file; every engine starts at the catalog to discover a table, so the catalog's pointer, not a storage path, defines what the table currently is.

The catalog is what makes commits atomic: a write produces a complete new metadata file, then asks the catalog to swap the current-metadata pointer; the swap is a compare-and-swap that succeeds only if the pointer still references the metadata the writer started from, so concurrent writers cannot silently overwrite each other.

Different catalog implementations realize the atomic swap differently — Hive Metastore with a conditional update on the metadata-location property, AWS Glue with a version-ID check, Nessie with a commit-hash check — but the contract to the engine is identical.

The Iceberg REST Catalog specification is an open, language-agnostic OpenAPI definition covering namespace and table management, an assertion-based (lock-free) commit protocol, view management, server-side scan planning, and credential vending; by 2025-2026 it had become the de facto interoperability layer that all major engines and managed catalogs speak.

Apache Polaris is the leading open-source REST catalog implementation: originated at Snowflake, donated to the ASF in August 2024, v1.0 (incubating) in July 2025, with releases through 1.7.0 by late 2026; it adds role-based access control and short-lived storage credential vending on top of the REST spec, and Snowflake Open Catalog is a managed Polaris service.

Project Nessie brings Git-like semantics to the catalog itself — branches, tags, and commits that can span many tables — so a set of changes across tables can be made on a branch and merged into main atomically, approximating multi-table transactions that core Iceberg lacks.

Cloud-managed catalogs dominate turnkey deployments as of October 2026: AWS Glue Data Catalog and Amazon S3 Tables (a bucket type with a REST-compatible catalog plus automatic compaction, snapshot expiry, and orphan cleanup), Databricks Unity Catalog (an Iceberg REST endpoint with read/write to Unity-managed Iceberg tables, public preview), and Snowflake Open Catalog.

Because every engine must pass through the catalog to find and commit to tables, the catalog is the natural single point for authentication, authorization, auditing, and credential issuance — which is why catalog choice, not file format, became the main competitive battleground of the lakehouse.

Choosing a catalog means choosing where governance lives, who vends storage credentials, and how hard it is to leave: REST-spec compliance keeps the protocol portable, but catalog state — grants, namespaces, audit history, maintenance policies — does not migrate automatically between catalogs.

Scene seed: the catalog is the library's card index at the front desk — no one walks the stacks (object storage) looking for a book; you ask the index for the current shelf location of the latest edition, and returns and new acquisitions are recorded at that one desk, one at a time — grounded in the fact that engines resolve name-to-metadata-pointer via the catalog and all commits serialize at that pointer.

pitfalls: Treating the catalog as a configuration detail: data files are portable, but grants, namespaces, and audit history live in the catalog, so swapping catalogs later is a real migration project.
Assuming 'REST catalog' names a product — it is a protocol; implementations differ widely in authentication, governance features, maintenance automation, and pricing.
Registering the same table location in two catalogs: only one catalog can own the atomic pointer, so dual registration forks the table's history or corrupts it.

Carrying the Hive mental model forward: the directory path no longer defines the table; writing files into the 'table folder' outside a commit adds nothing to the table (and deleting them can break it).

claims.text: An Iceberg table lives entirely on commodity object storage — Amazon S3, Azure ADLS, Google Cloud Storage, or S3-compatible on-prem stores — as ordinary files; Iceberg requires no storage service of its own, only a convention for tracking which files constitute the table.

Iceberg was designed around object-store weaknesses: it never relies on directory listing or file rename to define table state; all change happens by writing new immutable files plus one atomic pointer swap in the catalog, avoiding the slow listings and non-atomic renames that made Hive tables unreliable on S3.

Data files are typically Apache Parquet (Avro and ORC are also supported by the spec); columnar layout means a query reads only the columns it needs and benefits from heavy compression and per-row-group statistics.

The metadata forms a tree: catalog pointer -> table metadata file (JSON holding schema history, partition specs, snapshot log, properties) -> one manifest list per snapshot (Avro) -> manifest files (Avro, each listing data and delete files with partition values and per-column statistics) -> data files; every layer is immutable, and a new snapshot reuses unchanged manifests.

Metadata is what makes planning fast: engines prune in stages without touching data — manifest-list partition summaries skip whole manifests, per-file min/max and null counts in manifests skip individual files (e.g. a filter amount > 500 skips files whose max amount is 400), and Parquet row-group stats prune inside surviving files; planning cost scales with metadata size, never with a directory listing.

Metadata itself accumulates: every commit adds a snapshot, a manifest list, and usually new manifests, so high-frequency small commits (typical of streaming ingestion) grow both small data files and metadata, and query planning slows as manifests proliferate.

Maintenance is part of the table lifecycle, not an afterthought: compacting small files toward a target size (commonly 128-512 MB), expiring old snapshots, removing orphan files, and rewriting manifests; managed services increasingly automate this — S3 Tables runs compaction, snapshot expiry, and orphan cleanup in the background, AWS Glue's table optimizer triggers compaction when partitions exceed file-count thresholds, and Unity Catalog's predictive optimization handles compaction and snapshot expiration for managed Iceberg tables.

Format v3 (GA with Iceberg 1.10 in 2025, adopted across Snowflake, AWS, and Databricks during 2025-2026) changes the file layer: binary deletion vectors — compact bitmaps attached to data files — replace position-delete files, and row-lineage fields give each row a stable ID and last-updated sequence number; v3 readers can read v2 tables but not vice versa.

Scene seed: the metadata tree is a warehouse's inventory ledger — the ledger (manifests) records what each sealed crate (data file) contains, the range printed on its label (min/max stats), and the aisle it sits in (partition), so the picker plans the entire route at the front office without opening a single crate — grounded in manifest-based pruning replacing file listing and footer reads.
