catalog entry: db.orders -> s3://lake/orders/metadata/00012-abc.metadata.json
  00012-abc.metadata.json   (schemas, partition specs, snapshot log)
    └─ snap-9871.avro              manifest list for current snapshot
        ├─ manifest-a1.avro        -> 140 data files (2026-09 partitions, col min/max)
        └─ manifest-b2.avro        -> 6 data files + 2 delete files (2026-10)
            └─ data/.../file-0001.parquet
snippets.note: The four-layer metadata tree from catalog pointer to Parquet file; structure verified against the Iceberg table spec and Dremio's manifest walkthrough.

pitfalls: Believing Iceberg 'solves' the small-files problem — it tracks small files efficiently but does not prevent them; streaming and frequent batch commits still require compaction.
Deleting or moving files directly in the bucket corrupts the table: any file referenced by a live snapshot must only be removed through table maintenance operations.
Min/max statistics only prune well when data is sorted or clustered on the filter columns; randomly distributed values make every file's range overlap the query, and pruning silently stops helping.
Forgetting that metadata is also just files in the bucket — losing the current metadata.json or mis-scoping permissions on the metadata prefix breaks the table even when every data file is intact.

claims.text: Because table state lives in open files plus an open catalog protocol, multiple engines can read and write the same Iceberg table concurrently, with correctness guaranteed by the format's optimistic commit protocol rather than by any single engine's lock manager.

Engine landscape as of October 2026: Spark has the fullest support (DDL, DML, procedures, streaming); Flink does streaming and batch read/write; Trino's Iceberg connector supports full read/write SQL; Dremio supports read/write plus table maintenance; Snowflake reads and writes both Snowflake-managed and externally managed Iceberg tables; BigQuery supports managed 'BigLake tables for Apache Iceberg' plus external Iceberg reads.

DuckDB illustrates how far lightweight engines have come: its iceberg extension gained write support (CREATE TABLE, INSERT) via attached REST catalogs in DuckDB 1.4 (September 2025) and UPDATE/DELETE in subsequent 1.4.x releases, while direct metadata-path reads remain read-only — a laptop process can now safely commit to the same table a Spark cluster maintains.

The Iceberg spec is Apache-governed with explicit format versions; interoperability in practice depends on every participating engine supporting the table's format version and features — v3 readers read v2 tables, but v2-only engines cannot read v3 tables with deletion vectors or row lineage.

The REST catalog protocol is what makes multi-engine setups practical: one discovery, commit, and credential interface replaces per-engine catalog plugins, so the same table served by Polaris, S3 Tables, Unity Catalog, or Nessie is reachable from Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, Snowflake, and Dremio with configuration rather than code.

Apache XTable (incubating since February 2024) translates table metadata between Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Hudi without rewriting data files (release 0.4.0 added Paimon and plain-Parquet sources), reflecting an industry convergence in which one physical dataset can present as multiple formats.

Openness is often asymmetric in practice: Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint gives external engines read/write access to Unity-managed Iceberg tables and read-only access to Delta tables via UniForm, while Iceberg tables managed by foreign catalogs are read-only inside Databricks — 'supports Iceberg' can mean very different directions of freedom.

Lock-in does not disappear with an open format; it moves up the stack: storage and table format are commoditized, so differentiation and stickiness concentrate in the catalog, governance, and managed-maintenance layer.

Openness is a strategic choice with a real alternative: for a small team on a single engine with no multi-tool requirement, a managed proprietary platform can cost less to operate than self-managed open infrastructure — the value of Iceberg's openness compounds with the number of engines, teams, and years involved.

Scene seed: the ISO shipping container — Iceberg does not make ships, trains, and cranes interchangeable in capability, but any port can handle any container, so goods stop being repacked at every border; likewise data stops being copied and re-formatted at every tool boundary — grounded in one physical table serving Spark, Trino, Snowflake, and DuckDB simultaneously through the REST protocol.

pitfalls: 'Supports Iceberg' on a vendor datasheet often means read-only, or restricted to certain catalogs, format versions, or delete-file handling — always verify the write path and the feature matrix, not the checkbox.

Multi-engine writes to one table are safe for correctness but can conflict operationally: a long compaction job and a high-frequency streaming writer will force each other into commit retries; schedule maintenance away from hot write windows.
Adopting Iceberg does not by itself prevent lock-in — a proprietary catalog holding your grants, lineage, and maintenance policies can recreate the walled garden one layer up.

Interoperability is tested at the write path: nearly every engine reads Iceberg well, so differences (and production incidents) surface in what each engine can write — delete strategies, partition transforms, and format versions.

claims.text: Iceberg provides ACID-style guarantees per table commit: a commit either applies in full or is invisible, because the only way table state changes is the atomic swap of the catalog's metadata pointer — there is no intermediate state a reader can observe.
Readers get snapshot isolation for free: a query plans against one immutable snapshot and sees that consistent version for its entire run, no matter how many writers commit while it executes.

Writers use optimistic concurrency: each writer prepares new data and metadata files assuming the current snapshot will not change, then commits via compare-and-swap; on losing the race it re-validates its changes against the refreshed table state and retries, so no locks are held during the (possibly long) write.

Row-level operations (UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE) support two isolation levels: serializable fails the operation if any concurrent commit added files that might contain rows matching its condition, while snapshot isolation is more permissive; plain appends never produce data conflicts.

Commit conflicts and validation conflicts are different failure classes: a pointer race is harmless and resolved by automatic, tunable retries, while overlapping data changes fail validation regardless of retry settings — the fix is designing writers to touch disjoint partitions or rows.

The contrast with Hive-style tables explains why this matters: when table state was defined by listing directories, consumers could see half-loaded data, renames were non-atomic on object stores, and there was no atomicity across partitions; Iceberg removes the entire class of 'half-loaded table' incidents by construction.

Write-audit-publish (WAP) stages data like code: with write.wap.enabled set, a pipeline writes to a named branch (spark.wap.branch), quality checks run against the branch while main is untouched and consumers see nothing, and after checks pass the branch is published by fast-forwarding main to it; branch-based WAP has been the recommended pattern since Iceberg 1.2.

Retained history doubles as a recovery mechanism: because old snapshots persist until expired, a bad publish is undone by rolling the table back to a previous snapshot in seconds, instead of re-running pipelines or restoring backups.

Iceberg schemas function as enforceable data contracts: the schema is versioned in table metadata with stable field IDs, engines validate writes against it, and changes happen through explicit evolution operations — the table's interface to consumers changes deliberately, never by whatever files happen to land.

Scene seed: WAP is a newspaper's editorial workflow — reporters file into the proof pages (the branch), editors fact-check the proofs while yesterday's edition stays on the newsstand (main), and only an approved edition is printed, as one act (fast-forward); readers never see a half-edited page — grounded in branch writes being invisible on main until an atomic fast-forward.

snippets.code:
ALTER TABLE lake.db.events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled'='true');
-- each run writes to its own branch (Spark session: SET spark.wap.branch = etl_run_42)
INSERT INTO lake.db.events SELECT ...;            -- lands on branch, invisible on main
SELECT count(*) FROM lake.db.events.branch_etl_run_42
WHERE event_time IS NULL;                          -- audit the staged data
CALL lake.system.fast_forward('db.events', 'main', 'etl_run_42');  -- publish atomically
snippets.note: The three WAP steps (write to branch, audit branch, fast-forward main) as Spark SQL; flow verified against Iceberg branching docs and Dremio/lakeFS WAP walkthroughs.

pitfalls: Iceberg's ACID guarantees are per table: core Iceberg has no cross-table transactions, so multi-table consistency needs catalog-level branching (Nessie-style) or careful pipeline orchestration.
fast_forward fails if main advanced after the branch was created — concurrent pipelines publishing to one table need a rebase/cherry-pick strategy, not just WAP.
Optimistic concurrency degrades under very high commit frequency on one table (retry storms burn compute); batch commits or funnel hot tables through a single writer.
Stale WAP branches silently pin every file they reference, blocking snapshot expiration and growing storage — give audit branches an expiry and clean them up.

claims.text: In an open lakehouse the catalog is the natural control point for governance: every engine must ask it for table metadata and commit through it, so authentication, authorization, and audit logging centralize at the catalog instead of being re-implemented per engine.

Credential vending replaces shared bucket keys: a REST catalog issues short-lived, down-scoped storage credentials per request, limited to the specific table paths and operations the principal is allowed — a read-only grant yields credentials that can GetObject but not PutObject or DeleteObject.

Apache Polaris models access as RBAC with two role types — principal roles granted to service principals, and catalog roles carrying privileges (such as TABLE_READ_DATA, TABLE_WRITE_DATA) on catalogs, namespaces, and tables — giving table-level granularity across every connected engine.

As of 2026, catalog-enforced security is table-grained: open REST catalogs (Polaris through 1.7) cannot enforce row filtering or column masking, so fine-grained policies are enforced by engines or a policy layer, and once an engine holds vended file credentials it can physically read every column in those files.

Managed catalogs bundle finer-grained governance inside their own perimeter: Unity Catalog adds row filters, column masks, lineage, and audit for access through Databricks, and AWS pairs Glue/S3 Tables with Lake Formation permissions — currently the strongest row/column control comes from staying inside one vendor's enforcement path.

Snapshots make tables auditable by construction: every change is a recorded snapshot with operation summary, timestamp, and engine-supplied commit metadata, and time travel lets an auditor query the table exactly as it stood on a past date without restoring anything.

Deletion for privacy is a multi-step physical process: a DELETE only makes rows invisible in new snapshots, and the data persists in older snapshots and files until snapshot expiration plus orphan-file cleanup physically remove it — real GDPR-style erasure is delete, then expire, then purge.

Audit history and the right to erasure pull in opposite directions: a time-travel window that includes PII cannot be kept intact once those records must be destroyed; practical patterns include short retention on PII tables, isolating PII into separate tables or columns, and crypto-shredding (destroying per-subject encryption keys).

Data-product ownership maps cleanly onto catalog structure: namespaces group a domain's tables, grants define the product's consumers, the versioned schema is its interface, and snapshot history is its audit trail — the catalog becomes the registry where a data product's contract, policy, and provenance live together.

Scene seed: credential vending is a hotel front desk issuing a one-night key card for a single room instead of handing guests the master key — grounded in catalogs minting short-lived storage tokens scoped to one table's paths and to the operations the grant allows.

pitfalls: Anyone with direct bucket credentials bypasses every catalog policy; governance only holds if storage access is locked down so the catalog's vended credentials are the only path to the files.
Assuming DELETE satisfies an erasure request — deleted rows remain queryable via time travel until snapshots expire and the underlying files are physically purged.

Row and column policies defined in one engine do not travel with the table; an engine added later through the same open catalog may silently ignore them, so inventory every access path before granting it.

Governance retrofitted after broad adoption rarely sticks: once teams hold bucket paths and ad-hoc keys, revoking them is technically and politically hard — build the catalog-grant path in from day one.

claims.text: Iceberg was created at Netflix by Ryan Blue and Dan Weeks to make petabyte-scale analytic tables on object storage reliable, and was donated to the Apache Software Foundation in 2018; its design assumptions (immutable files, snapshot metadata, planning without directory listings) target high-volume analytical data.

By 2025 every major analytics platform could read and write Iceberg tables — Snowflake announced full read/write support in April 2025, Databricks made Iceberg first-class in Unity Catalog after acquiring Tabular, Google added BigQuery/BigLake Iceberg support, and AWS ships native support across S3 Tables, Glue, Athena, EMR, and Redshift — which is what makes Iceberg fit multi-team, multi-engine architectures.

One Iceberg table can be fed by batch Spark jobs, Flink streaming jobs committing at checkpoints, and a configuration-driven Kafka Connect sink, so batch and streaming ingestion converge on the same governed dataset.

Iceberg fits auditable, reproducible data products: snapshots give a complete version history, tags preserve important historical states (the docs name auditing and GDPR retention as intended uses), and branches isolate experiments — capabilities that also serve ML training-set versioning.

Iceberg is explicitly not an OLTP system: Cloudera's guidance states it is not designed for high-frequency transactions and that its row-level UPDATE/DELETE are unsuitable for operational transactional workloads, recommending it for large, relatively slowly changing datasets; single-row low-latency work belongs in databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL.

For very small datasets Iceberg's machinery is overhead rather than benefit: practitioner reviews note the format was designed for petabyte scale, and its extra indirection layers and nested metadata add friction when the biggest table fits on a laptop.
Iceberg's commit model is batch/micro-batch oriented, so it is a poor choice where consumers need sub-second data freshness or point-lookup serving latency.

A single-engine shop captures less of Iceberg's value, since engine interoperability is one of its principal advantages; a managed warehouse may remain simpler if no second engine or team is in sight.

Production evidence spans industries and scales: Netflix runs write-audit-publish quality gates across thousands of Iceberg tables, LinkedIn's OpenHouse control plane managed 3,500+ Iceberg tables with 550+ daily active users at open-sourcing (talks since cite 100K+ table deployments), and Shopify standardized its centralized lakehouse on Iceberg queried by Trino.

Scene seed: after a period of intense scaling, Shopify found data silos had formed around incompatible table formats and tools; standardizing all lakehouse data on Iceberg behind Trino restored interoperability and cut some query workloads from hours to seconds — a concrete picture of 'one table format, many engines'.

pitfalls: Expecting Iceberg to make small data fast — at laptop scale the metadata layers add latency and operational burden, not performance.
Treating Iceberg's row-level updates as a license to run operational/transactional workloads on it; high-frequency single-row writes belong in an OLTP database.
Adopting the format without a shared catalog — if each engine keeps its own catalog, the silos the format was meant to dissolve simply reappear one level up.
Ignoring the standing maintenance cost: compaction, snapshot expiry, and orphan-file cleanup are mandatory operations, so every table needs an owner.

claims.text: A typical Iceberg reporting architecture layers raw ingestion tables, transformation into curated tables, and BI consumption; because every Iceberg write is one atomic snapshot commit, downstream consumers never observe a partially loaded table even mid-job.

Scheduled loads become idempotent with dynamic-partition INSERT OVERWRITE: a rerun atomically replaces exactly the partitions the job produces and leaves all others untouched, so retrying a failed daily load cannot duplicate data.

Late or corrected data is handled with MERGE INTO, which matches source rows to target rows and updates, deletes, or inserts accordingly; Iceberg rewrites only the data files actually affected, and the official docs recommend MERGE INTO over INSERT OVERWRITE for row-level changes.

The write-audit-publish (WAP) pattern — write new data where consumers cannot see it, audit it with quality checks, then publish atomically — was popularized by Netflix in a 2017 DataWorks Summit talk and is natively supported in Iceberg via staging branches and the fast_forward procedure.

Netflix runs WAP across thousands of Iceberg tables: pipelines write to a hidden snapshot or branch, an internal auditor tool validates it, and only a passing audit exposes the data — with no copying of data during the audit step.

A bad pipeline run is reversible without restoring backups: the rollback_to_snapshot procedure points the table back at a prior snapshot, and cherrypick_snapshot/publish_changes apply a staged change under controlled publication.

The history and snapshots metadata tables record every table version with its operation and writer metadata (including the engine application ID), so 'why did the numbers change overnight?' is answerable with a SQL join rather than log archaeology.

Writers no longer hand-manage file layout: since Iceberg 1.2 the default write.distribution-mode=hash shuffles rows by partition automatically, and range distribution is used when the table defines a sort order — the table spec drives physical layout, not per-job code.

Scene seed: a finance team closes the books — the month-end load lands on an audit branch, reconciliation checks run against it, fast_forward publishes it, and a tag like 'EOY-2023' retained forever preserves the exact audited numbers while daily loads continue on main.

snippets.code:
-- Late-arriving corrections folded into a curated sales table
MERGE INTO prod.sales.daily_revenue t
USING updates_batch s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.amount = s.amount, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
snippets.note: Row-level upsert for late/corrected data; Iceberg rewrites only affected files. Verified against the official Spark Writes docs (MERGE INTO section).
The documented audit-branch WAP flow: stage, validate, publish by fast-forwarding main. Verified against the official Branching and Tagging docs.

pitfalls: Static INSERT OVERWRITE (Spark's default mode) with no PARTITION clause replaces the entire table; the docs recommend dynamic partition-overwrite mode for Iceberg.
MERGE INTO errors out when one target row matches multiple source rows, so source batches must be deduplicated by the merge key first.
A rerun that appends instead of overwriting or merging silently duplicates data — idempotency is a design decision, not an Iceberg default.
Frequent scheduled loads still accumulate small files and snapshots; compaction and expire_snapshots belong inside the pipeline's operating model, not as an afterthought.

claims.text: The Flink Iceberg sink guarantees exactly-once delivery by committing an Iceberg snapshot only after a successful Flink checkpoint (in the notifyCheckpointComplete callback); on restart the job resumes from the last committed snapshot, whose checkpoint ID is stored in the snapshot summary.

Latency in an Iceberg streaming pipeline is bounded by the commit interval: each checkpoint or micro-batch trigger produces one snapshot, official docs recommend trigger intervals of at least one minute, and the result is 'minutes-fresh' analytics, not sub-second serving.

Frequent commits mean small files and metadata growth — a 60-second trigger is 1,440 commits per day — so streaming tables require routine rewrite_data_files compaction, rewrite_manifests (streaming uses fast appends that skip manifest compaction), and regular expire_snapshots.

For CDC from operational databases, Flink's upsert mode applies updates and deletes from a changelog stream; it requires a format-v2 table with identifier (primary key) fields, and for partitioned tables the partition source columns must be included in the equality fields.

Streaming CDC writers favor equality deletes because they need no read-before-write, but the deferred merge cost moves to readers: query performance degrades as delete files accumulate until compaction rewrites them (format v3 can convert equality deletes to deletion vectors).

The Apache Iceberg Kafka Connect sink offers code-free streaming ingestion with exactly-once semantics via centralized commit coordination over a control topic (default commit interval 5 minutes), including fan-out routing of one topic into multiple tables.

Iceberg tables are streaming sources too: Spark Structured Streaming can read incrementally from a table starting at a timestamp (append snapshots only, with per-micro-batch file/row rate limits), and the create_changelog_view procedure exposes a table's changes — including net changes and pre/post-update images — to downstream incremental consumers.

Exactly-once sinks eliminate duplicates from failures and restarts, but duplicates originating upstream (at-least-once producers, replayed CDC) still require key-based handling — upsert mode in the sink or deduplicating MERGE downstream.

Scene seed: a clickstream pipeline committing every minute turns the table into a flipbook of 1,440 versions a day — each snapshot a consistent frame of the business — which is also why Netflix-scale operations pair streaming ingestion with automated compaction services and commit-lag alerting.

snippets.note: Upsert mode via SQL hint; requires identifier fields on a v2 table. Commits happen at Flink checkpoints. Verified against the official Flink Writes docs.

pitfalls: Chasing freshness by shortening the checkpoint/trigger interval multiplies snapshots and small files, and the compaction bill grows faster than the latency benefit.
Expiring snapshots or deleting orphan files too aggressively can corrupt a running Flink job's recovery: keep the last snapshot the job committed (identified by flink.job-id in the snapshot summary).
Iceberg commits can fail even while Flink checkpoints succeed, so monitor commit lag (elapsedSecondsSinceLastSuccessfulCommit) separately from checkpoint health.
Upsert-mode equality deletes silently degrade read performance as they accumulate; without scheduled compaction the table gets slower every day it runs.

claims.text: Every write to an Iceberg table creates an immutable snapshot with an ID and timestamp, so a training dataset's exact historical state can be queried months later without storing a separate copy — dataset versioning is a property of the table rather than an extra system.

Reproducible training means pinning the data alongside code and hyperparameters: teams log the Iceberg snapshot ID (for example as an MLflow run attribute) with the model artifact, and retraining reads the identical rows with VERSION AS OF that snapshot.

Tags make dataset pins durable: a named tag such as a model-version label is a retained reference that survives routine snapshot expiration according to its own retention policy, unlike a bare snapshot ID.

Time travel provides point-in-time correctness for features, preventing leakage of future information into training sets; without it teams manually track feature-computation timestamps and build complex join logic to avoid leakage.

Netflix's Axion fact store — the primary data source for its personalization ML models — stores logged raw facts in Iceberg tables (paired with EVCache for low-latency access) and regenerates features from facts on demand, cutting experiment data preparation from weeks of feature logging to hours.
PyIceberg gives Python-native, JVM-free access to Iceberg tables (scans to Arrow, pandas, DuckDB), connecting lakehouse tables directly to ML tooling such as notebooks, Ray, and PyTorch data loaders.

Corrections and retraining are first-class: row-level updates fix mislabeled records and deletes honor erasure requests, each producing a new auditable snapshot, while create_changelog_view shows exactly which rows changed between two training runs.

Branches support dataset experimentation: a candidate training or evaluation set can be built and validated on a branch without touching the production lineage, then merged forward or discarded — the same mechanics used for data quality gates.

Scene seed: when a six-month-old churn model comes under review, one query — SELECT ... VERSION AS OF the tag recorded at training time — reproduces its exact training table, the data-side equivalent of checking out the Git commit a binary was built from.

snippets.note: Tag-then-time-travel pattern for reproducible training data. Syntax verified against the official Branching/Tagging and Spark Queries docs.

pitfalls: Pinning a bare snapshot ID is fragile: expire_snapshots can remove it and break reproducibility — use tags with explicit retention for anything a model depends on.
A snapshot pins only the data; reproducibility still requires versioning the feature code, hyperparameters, and environment alongside the snapshot reference.
Branch reads use the table's current schema while tag and snapshot-ID reads use the snapshot's schema — a subtle difference that can change feature pipelines' column sets.

Privacy erasure and perfect reproducibility conflict: after a GDPR delete, the 'exact' historical training set legally must change, so record that divergence rather than pretending the snapshot is still intact.

claims.text: Time travel turns audits and investigations into queries: TIMESTAMP AS OF / VERSION AS OF reconstruct the table as a regulator or incident responder would have seen it, and the history and snapshots metadata tables record every version with its operation and writer metadata (including the engine application ID).

The official docs recommend tags for audit retention — e.g. an end-of-year tag retained forever or an end-of-week tag retained 7 days — and explicitly name GDPR-driven retention policies as a use case for tag-level lifecycle control.

The audit window is bounded by snapshot retention: expire_snapshots permanently removes old versions and the files only they reference (common defaults keep about five days of history), so time-travel depth is a policy decision compliance teams must set per table, not an unlimited free feature.

Right-to-erasure is a two-step process on Iceberg: a DELETE is logical — position/equality delete files (or v3 deletion vectors) mask rows at read time while the bytes remain in data files and in every earlier snapshot — and physical erasure happens only after snapshot expiration plus compaction rewrite the affected files.

Under merge-on-read, 'deleted' rows remain byte-for-byte readable in current data files until compaction runs, and further copies can persist in replicas, backups, and object-store version history — all outside what a SQL DELETE touches.

Branches put governance in the write path: the documented audit-branch workflow (write.wap.enabled, write to a staging branch, validate, fast_forward main) means bad or unreviewed data is never visible to consumers — the pattern Netflix applies across thousands of production tables.

Controlled publication has reversal primitives to match: rollback_to_snapshot undoes a published mistake, and cherrypick_snapshot / publish_changes promote a specific staged change by its WAP ID — change management for data analogous to release management for code.

Iceberg tables scale into governed data products when paired with a control plane: LinkedIn's OpenHouse layers a declarative REST catalog plus data services (maintenance, retention, sharing policy) over Iceberg tables, with 3,500+ managed production tables and 550+ daily active users at open-sourcing in 2024.

Scene seed: a regulator asks what the risk table said on March 31; instead of restoring a warehouse backup to a scratch environment, the team answers with one AS OF query against the quarter-close tag — the audit trail was the table all along.

snippets.note: Audit tag + time travel, and the logical-then-physical erasure sequence. Syntax verified against the official Branching/Tagging, Spark Queries, and Spark Procedures docs; erasure sequence per Dremio's right-to-be-forgotten analysis.

pitfalls: A DELETE alone is not erasure: the data persists in older snapshots, in merge-on-read data files until compaction, and in backups and object-store versioning that Iceberg does not control.
Long time-travel retention for audit and short retention for privacy pull in opposite directions; without a per-table retention policy one requirement silently violates the other.
A forever-retained tag pins every data file its snapshot references, so an audit tag on a table containing personal data can indefinitely preserve rows that were later 'deleted'.
Snapshot history shows what changed and when, but it is not access control or lineage by itself — who may read which rows and columns still comes from the catalog and governance layer.

claims.text: An Iceberg lakehouse reference architecture has six recurring layers: object storage holding data and metadata files; a catalog for table discovery and atomic commits; ingestion (batch loads, streaming, CDC, file drops); transformation engines; consumption (BI, interactive SQL, ML); and governance spanning all of them.

The medallion (bronze/silver/gold) layering maps directly onto Iceberg: bronze holds raw data exactly as it arrives (append-only, replayable via snapshots), silver holds cleansed and conformed data maintained with MERGE for CDC and corrections, and gold holds curated business-level aggregates for consumption.

Because the table format and catalog are shared, engines can be chosen per workload rather than per platform: Spark-class engines for large batch transformation and table maintenance, Flink-class for streaming ingestion, Trino/BigQuery-class for interactive and high-concurrency SQL, and DuckDB-class for local or small-scale analysis — all reading and writing the same tables.

Catalogs address tables hierarchically (catalog.namespace.table); namespaces are the natural unit for organizing tables by data domain and by medallion layer, and they double as the unit for access control and ownership boundaries.

Catalog choice is the most strategic design decision: catalogs that implement the open Iceberg REST catalog specification stay portable across engines and vendors, and modern catalogs can federate to remote external catalogs (e.g. Unity Catalog or AWS Glue) rather than forcing one vendor's control plane.

A table's physical design decisions — partition spec, sort order, copy-on-write vs merge-on-read, target file size — should be made per table from its query and write patterns at design time, because they drive both query cost (request counts, planning time) and maintenance burden later.

Maintenance must be designed in from day one: every production table needs an owner and a plan for compaction, snapshot expiration, and orphan-file cleanup, either self-run or delegated to managed services such as Amazon S3 Tables or Glue catalog optimization that automate these tasks.

An architect's decision checklist distilled from reference guidance: (1) workloads and latency needs, (2) engine mix per workload, (3) one catalog as the single source of truth, (4) namespace/domain layout and ownership, (5) per-table partitioning and update strategy, (6) maintenance automation and its owner, (7) access control and governance model, (8) cost model covering storage, compute, and object-store requests.

Scene seed: a lakehouse is a city plan — object storage is the land, tables are the buildings, namespaces are zoned districts (one per data domain), the catalog is the official address registry every service consults, and engines are the utilities that plug into any building; the registry analogy is literal, since every engine resolves a table through the catalog before touching storage.

snippets.code:
-- Namespaces as domain + layer boundaries
CREATE NAMESPACE lake.sales_silver;
CREATE TABLE lake.sales_silver.orders (
  order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT,
  order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DECIMAL(12,2))
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(order_ts));
snippets.note: Standard Spark SQL against an Iceberg catalog: tables addressed as catalog.namespace.table, with the namespace carrying the domain/layer; verified against Iceberg Spark DDL docs and Google Cloud lakehouse key-concepts docs.

pitfalls: Copying a warehouse schema layout one-to-one into the lakehouse and skipping namespace/domain design leaves no ownership or access-control boundaries to govern later.
Choosing engines first and the catalog last inverts the real dependency: a proprietary catalog can lock in the whole architecture even though the table format is open.
Partitioning every large table by date out of habit, instead of by actual query predicates, bakes in poor pruning that partition evolution can fix only for future data.
Designing only the write path: a table with no planned compaction and expiration owner degrades slowly and invisibly until queries and bills spike.

claims.text: Maintaining an Iceberg table means four recurring jobs, each countering a distinct kind of growth: rewrite_data_files (compacts small data files), expire_snapshots (prunes old table versions and the files only they reference), rewrite_manifests (consolidates metadata for faster planning), and remove_orphan_files (deletes files no snapshot references, left by failed jobs).

Every commit creates a snapshot, so snapshots accumulate continuously; the official docs recommend regularly expiring snapshots, which deletes data files that are no longer needed and shrinks metadata — the defaults keep roughly 5 days of history (older_than default: 5 days ago) and retain at least 1 snapshot.

Streaming and frequent micro-batch writes are the main small-file factory: writers emit files per task per partition per commit, so a job committing every minute can generate tens of thousands of small files per day; compaction rewrites them toward the table's target file size (write.target-file-size-bytes, 512 MB by default) using binpack, sort, or z-order strategies.

Small files are a cost problem, not just a speed problem: in a worked example, a 100,000-file table needs on the order of 200,000 GET requests per full scan and 15–30 seconds of planning, versus under a second and ~93% lower request cost after compacting to ~2,000 right-sized files.

Commit frequency has its own cost floor: every commit writes a new manifest, manifest list, and metadata.json regardless of how little data it carries, and metadata.json is rewritten whole — so commit overhead scales with table metadata size, which is why batching writes matters as much as compacting files.

remove_orphan_files cleans up files abandoned by failed or killed jobs; by default it only considers files older than 3 days, and the docs warn that shortening that interval risks corrupting the table by deleting files belonging to in-progress writes — hence the dry-run-first convention.

rewrite_manifests speeds query planning by consolidating metadata: each manifest is a separate object-store read during planning, so cutting a table from 500 manifests to 20 removes 480 I/O round trips from every query plan.

Table health is observable with plain SQL because Iceberg exposes metadata tables (snapshots, files, partitions, manifests, history): common checks are average file size per partition (compact when it drops below a threshold), per-partition file counts, and snapshot-count growth; since Iceberg 1.2, metrics reporters offer push-based monitoring for REST and JDBC catalogs.

Maintenance is increasingly a managed service: Amazon S3 Tables runs compaction, snapshot management, and unreferenced-file removal automatically (defaults: 512 MB target file size, minimum 1 snapshot retained, 120-hour maximum snapshot age), and AWS Glue offers managed compaction for Parquet Iceberg tables that runs without blocking concurrent queries.

Scene seed: table maintenance is cleaning a shared kitchen — every pipeline run leaves dishes (small files), the fridge fills with dated leftovers (old snapshots), and unlabeled containers accumulate that nobody claims (orphan files); the docs' answer is the same as a good kitchen's: a posted rota (scheduled maintenance jobs, in order: compact, expire, then remove orphans last) and a named owner.

snippets.code:
CALL catalog.system.expire_snapshots(
  table => 'db.sales',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-10-07 00:00:00',
  retain_last => 10);
snippets.note: Expires snapshots older than a cutoff while always keeping the 10 most recent; defaults are ~5 days and retain_last 1. Verified against Iceberg Spark procedures docs.

snippets.code:
CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.sales',
  strategy => 'binpack',
  where => 'order_ts >= DATE \'2026-10-01\'');
snippets.note: Compacts small files in recent partitions only; strategies are binpack (default), sort, and z-order. Verified against Iceberg Spark procedures docs.

pitfalls: Expiring snapshots is permanent: it deletes the files behind old versions, so time travel and rollback to those versions is gone — retention must be set from audit and recovery needs, not storage savings alone.
Running remove_orphan_files with an aggressive older_than window can delete files from in-flight writes and corrupt the table; the 3-day default and a dry run exist for a reason.
Storage grows right after compaction, surprising teams: rewritten data coexists with the old files until the snapshots referencing them expire, so 'cleanup' is a two-step process.
Assuming the format maintains itself: Iceberg ships the procedures but nothing schedules them — an unowned table degrades slowly until queries and object-store bills make it visible.

claims.text: There are two migration strategies: in-place migration writes Iceberg metadata over existing data files without moving or rewriting them (procedures: snapshot, migrate, add_files), while shadow (full-data) migration rewrites data into a brand-new Iceberg table via CTAS or a parallel pipeline — slower and costlier, but it allows restructuring (new partitioning, sorting, file sizes) and keeps the source untouched as a rollback.

The snapshot procedure creates a temporary Iceberg table under a new name that references the source Hive table's files; the source stays authoritative and writable, making it the standard way to test engines and pipelines against Iceberg before committing to migration.

The migrate procedure converts a Hive table in place, keeping its name so existing queries keep working; all writers must be stopped first, the source's files (Parquet/Avro/ORC only) are adopted as-is, and the original is kept as a renamed backup table.

The add_files procedure registers existing data files into an already-existing Iceberg table as a new snapshot without rewriting them; it is the building block for custom and incremental migrations, with the caveat that Hive-sourced files need a name mapping on the table (snapshot and migrate set this automatically).

Delta Lake tables migrate via the iceberg-delta-lake module's snapshotDeltaLakeTable action, which replays the Delta transaction log into the new Iceberg table as ordered commits — preserving history — while reusing the same Parquet data files; the module ships separately from the Spark/Flink runtimes.

There is no official Iceberg procedure for Hudi sources; the usual path is Apache XTable (incubating), which translates table metadata among Hudi, Delta, and Iceberg in either direction without rewriting data, supporting full and incremental sync modes.

Interop layers can defer migration entirely: Delta Lake UniForm asynchronously generates Iceberg metadata after each Delta commit so Iceberg clients can read the Delta table, which lets teams adopt Iceberg-reading engines before (or instead of) converting tables — but it is read-only from the Iceberg side.

Validating parity needs more than row counts: practitioner guidance is to run the legacy and Iceberg pipelines side by side (shadow), diff daily using checksums or business-level aggregate queries, and cut consumers over only after a sustained parity window (one documented heuristic: seven consecutive matching days).

A phased adoption roadmap recurs across guidance: start with new tables or one low-risk domain, prove the maintenance and governance operating model there, move read paths before write paths, keep the legacy path as rollback until parity holds, then decommission — the hard part being consumer cutover and organizational change (table ownership, catalog governance, new engine skills), not data movement.

Scene seed: in-place migration is recataloging a library without moving a single book — the shelves (data files) stay put and only the card catalog (metadata) is rewritten, which is literally what snapshot/migrate/add_files do; shadow migration is building a new library next door and moving readers over branch by branch while the old reading room stays open.

snippets.note: The documented two-step Hive migration pattern: snapshot to validate, migrate to convert in place keeping the table name. Verified against Iceberg Spark procedures and Hive migration docs.
Registers existing files into an Iceberg table as a new snapshot without rewriting data — the incremental/custom migration building block. Verified against Iceberg Spark procedures docs.

pitfalls: migrate replaces the source table in place and requires stopping all writers first; skipping the snapshot-based dry run or the writer freeze is the classic migration incident.
A snapshot table shares physical files with its source, so running remove_orphan_files (or expiring aggressively) on it can delete files the original table still depends on.
Metadata-translation interop (UniForm, XTable) gives read access, not write access — treating a translated table as writable from both formats risks one side's cleanup destroying the other's table.

Matching row counts do not prove parity (soft deletes, computed columns, and type coercion all hide drift); use checksums or business-aggregate diffs, and expect the 'temporary' dual-pipeline phase to become permanent unless cutover has a named owner and deadline.

claims.text: Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Hudi have converged on the same physical foundation — Parquet data files on object storage plus a metadata/log layer — and their feature sets are cross-pollinating: deletion vectors, pioneered in Delta, became part of the Iceberg v3 spec. Public proposals for Iceberg v4 even include a redesigned adaptive metadata tree that a future Delta version might share — still a community discussion, not a settled direction.

Iceberg format version 3 reached general availability with Apache Iceberg 1.10.0 (September 2025), adding binary deletion vectors, row lineage (stable row IDs that survive compaction), a VARIANT type for semi-structured data, geometry/geography types, nanosecond timestamps, default column values, and multi-argument partition transforms.

Format-version compatibility is one-directional: v3 readers can read v2 tables, but v2 readers cannot read v3 tables, and upgrading a table from v2 to v3 cannot be undone — so a v3 feature is only usable once every engine touching the table supports v3.

Two interoperability bridges let one copy of data serve multiple formats without rewriting it: Apache XTable (incubating; formerly OneTable, donated to the ASF in 2024) translates metadata among Hudi, Delta, and Iceberg with full and incremental sync, and Delta Lake UniForm generates Iceberg metadata asynchronously after each Delta commit (read-only for Iceberg clients).

2024 was the consolidation inflection point: Databricks — steward of Delta Lake — acquired Tabular, the company founded by Iceberg's creators, in June 2024 (reportedly over $1B), explicitly to pursue format interoperability; two months later Snowflake and Dremio donated the Polaris catalog to the Apache Software Foundation.

The competitive battleground has moved from table formats to catalogs, which are converging on the Iceberg REST catalog specification: Apache Polaris graduated to an ASF Top-Level Project in March 2026 (~100 contributors, 6 releases during incubation) and now also supports Delta; Databricks Unity Catalog implements the Iceberg REST APIs and federates external catalogs including AWS Glue and Snowflake Horizon; Glue ships an Iceberg REST adapter.

By 2026 every major platform offers managed Iceberg natively — Amazon S3 Tables with built-in automatic maintenance, Databricks managed Iceberg tables (v3 support) in Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon running its interoperability on Polaris with external-engine reads GA and writes in preview — making Iceberg the de facto interchange format of the lakehouse, with vendors differentiating on catalogs, engines, and operations rather than the format itself.

AI workloads are shaping the roadmap: v3's VARIANT and geospatial types, row lineage for reproducibility and incremental processing, and multi-engine single-copy access respond to ML and AI platforms needing governed, versioned training and feature data on the same tables analytics uses.

A durable evaluation rule falls out of the version mechanics: judge any new table-format feature by (1) whether it is in the adopted open spec rather than one vendor's extension, (2) whether every engine you run can read and write it, and (3) whether you need it — and upgrade format versions only when all three align, since upgrades are one-way.

Scene seed: table formats are going through a USB-C moment — rival connectors (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) converging on one port everyone can plug into, with Parquet-on-object-storage as the wire and the Iceberg REST catalog spec as the port shape, while vendors now compete on the devices (engines, catalogs, managed services) rather than the plug; the grounding is literal, since Polaris, Unity, Glue, and Horizon all implement the same REST specification.

snippets.code:
ALTER TABLE lake.sales.orders
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3');
snippets.note: The one-line, one-way upgrade to Iceberg v3 (requires Iceberg 1.10+ and v3-capable engines on every reader and writer). Verified against Iceberg v3 rollout coverage.

snippets.code:
sourceFormat: HUDI
targetFormats:
  - ICEBERG
  - DELTA
datasets:
  - tableBasePath: s3://lake/sales/orders
    tableName: orders
snippets.note: An Apache XTable sync config: one physical table exposed to readers of all three formats by translating metadata only. Verified against Apache XTable docs.

pitfalls: 'The format war is over' overstates it: convergence is real at the metadata and catalog layer, but write-side interop is still limited (UniForm is read-only from Iceberg, XTable translation lags the source), so one format must still own each table's writes.
A spec feature is not a usable feature: engines adopt format versions unevenly, and upgrading a table to v3 silently cuts off every v2-only reader with no downgrade path.

Because the format is open, teams treat catalog choice as a detail — but the catalog is where lock-in has moved; a catalog that does not speak the Iceberg REST spec re-creates the proprietary boundary the open format removed.

Evaluating formats by vendor benchmark posts invites whiplash; roadmaps shift with acquisitions and proposals (e.g. the v4 metadata-tree discussion), so architectures should bet on the spec and interop layers, not on any one quarter's feature race.
